title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral or bullet marker that begins an item in an enumerated list, typically a digit (2, 3, 4, 5, etc.) followed by a period, often paired with bold markdown formatting introducing a list entry. It activates on the token itself at the start of a list step, regardless of the surrounding topic (advice steps, instructions, rankings, tips). It does not activate on the prose content of the list items or on plain sentences lacking an explicit numbered/bulleted list structure, and is largely indifferent to subject matter, only tracking the structural position of enumeration markers.

title: Introducing a structured explanation
description: This latent fires on short lead-in phrases that preface an itemized or elaborated explanation, typically ending in a colon or immediately followed by a list or detailed breakdown (e.g., 'Here's a breakdown of...', 'Here's why', bolded headers like 'The bird has settled in with you**:'). It activates on the structural/formatting cue that signals 'what follows is a detailed explanation or enumerated reasoning,' rather than on the content of that explanation itself. It also captures framing clauses that set up a forthcoming analysis based on given context ('Given your current income and expenses'). It would not activate on the actual list items, explanatory content, or narrative sentences that lack this introductory, colon-preceding, structure-signaling role.

title: Wry framing exclamation opener
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic exclamatory openers that wryly label an upcoming interpersonal situation as a familiar 'type' before discussing it—typically patterned as 'The [age-old/classic/eternal] [noun] [drama/dilemma/conundrum/rivalry]!' It activates most strongly on these stock framing phrases themselves (e.g., 'The age-old sibling drama!', 'The classic roommate conundrum!'), especially in advice/AITA-style responses that open by categorizing a scenario with a knowing, slightly humorous tone. It does not activate on the substantive analysis, advice, or reasoning that follows (e.g., sentences about communication, compromise, or moral judgment), nor on plain empathetic statements or questions that lack this templated 'labeling exclamation' structure—even if they discuss the same topics of family or relationship conflict.

title: Referral to specific help resources
description: This latent fires on list-style recommendations that direct the reader to a named external resource, organization, hotline, or service category for help with a problem (e.g. crisis hotlines, credit counseling agencies, shelters, tutoring centers, gig-work platforms). It activates most strongly on bolded/itemized suggestion headers naming a concrete resource type or specific organization (National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, NFCC, Uber Eats, 2-1-1, etc.), typically in imperative or 'Consider X' phrasing within an enumerated advice list. It also weakly activates on generic list-numbering tokens and softer phrasings like 'there are many resources available.' It does NOT activate on general advice, reasoning about interpersonal situations, reflective commentary, or suggestions that don't point to an identifiable service/organization/resource (e.g. 'offer alternatives,' 'ask open-ended questions,' 'focus on your goals'), even when these appear in similarly formatted numbered lists.

title: Advice to have an open, honest conversation
description: This latent fires on advice-genre text that recommends resolving interpersonal conflict by initiating a calm, open, or honest conversation/communication—phrases like 'Have an open and honest conversation with...', 'By communicating openly', 'Try to have a calm and respectful conversation', and the list-item scaffolding (numbers like '2.', '3.', bolded headers like 'By having an') that introduces such suggestions in structured advice lists. It activates most strongly on the recurring templated phrase itself ('open and honest conversation', 'calm and respectful conversation', 'communicate your feelings') and on the numbered/bulleted markers that precede these recommendations, even when truncated to just 'By' or '2.'. It does NOT activate strongly on other relationship-advice content that doesn't invoke this specific communication-conversation framing—e.g., sentences about setting boundaries, weighing consequences, seeking a therapist, evaluating fault, or general empathetic statements—even though these appear in the same advice-column context, since the latent tracks the specific rhetorical move of prescribing dialogue/communication as the solution rather than advice content generally.

title: Charitable justification of behavior
description: This latent fires on sentences that offer a reasonable, benign explanation for someone's behavior that might otherwise seem suspicious or questionable, framing it as understandable given the context. It activates on statements that rationalize or normalize an action (e.g., contacting someone outside normal hours) by appealing to plausible circumstances like professional necessity or shared responsibilities. It would not activate on neutral factual descriptions of behavior without an accompanying justification, nor on sentences that express suspicion, criticism, or accusation rather than charitable interpretation.

title: Direct interpersonal questions/invitations (second-person)
description: This latent fires on short, direct, second-person conversational utterances addressed to a specific 'you' or 'we' — questions checking in on someone's well-being ('Is everything okay?'), proposing plans or alternatives ('Can we do something else?', 'Would you like to join us?'), or suggesting rescheduling/catching up ('Maybe we can catch up another time?'). It activates most strongly on these as standalone quoted or spoken lines, including truncated fragments ('Can I', 'Would you'), rather than on narrative or advisory prose. It does not activate on third-person descriptions, advice-giving statements about what someone 'should' or 'could' do, general reflections, or numbered lists/bullet instructions, even when discussing similar relational topics — the key trigger is the direct, quotable, question-or-invitation phrasing itself rather than the underlying relationship content.

title: Self-help advice list items on cognitive reframing
description: This latent fires on advice-list bullet points recommending mental/emotional coping strategies, especially those centered on reframing negative thoughts, positive self-talk, affirmations, mindfulness, and gratitude practices—often formatted as bolded imperative headers followed by a colon (e.g., 'Reframe negative self-talk**: Challenge negative thoughts...'). It also activates on short lead-in fragments like 'This can', 'This will help', or 'Practice' that typically precede or follow such advice, and on generic list-numbering artifacts. It does NOT activate strongly on advice about concrete behavioral/interpersonal actions (e.g., preparing for a conversation, using productivity tools, checking fees) or on descriptive/analytical statements about a situation, even when topically related to relationships or emotions—the key trigger is the specific cognitive-reframing/affirmation self-talk framing rather than advice-giving in general.

title: Conditional/motivational framing setup
description: This latent appears to fire on short clauses that establish a premise or emotional motivation preceding a main point or conclusion—e.g., a conditional opener ('If it...') or a statement of concern/care that sets up why an action matters ('You care about your friend's success...'). It activates on fragments or sentences that function as setup or justification rather than the payoff or conclusion itself, often signaling an upcoming consequence, recommendation, or explanation. It would not activate on purely declarative factual statements, direct conclusions, or sentences that state outcomes/results without framing them as contingent on or motivated by a prior condition or concern. Sentences that are self-contained assertions with no dependency clause or emotional/relational stake would not trigger it.

title: Asserting a reasonable expectation of others
description: This latent fires on statements that frame a normative expectation of behavior or effort from other people as being 'reasonable' or justified, often as a standard of fairness or comparison. It activates on sentences that express a claim about what is fair, appropriate, or expected of someone based on shared norms or comparable circumstances. It would not activate on purely descriptive statements about effort or behavior that lack this evaluative, expectation-setting framing, nor on expressions of personal preference or emotion unrelated to judging fairness or standards for others.

title: Judgmental condemnation of someone's behavior
description: This latent fires on evaluative verdict statements that label a person's reaction, tone, or comment as unacceptable, disproportionate, aggressive, harsh, hurtful, condescending, or otherwise inappropriate—typically in the pattern '[Person]'s [reaction/response/tone] was [negative judgment adjective]'. It activates most strongly on short, declarative moral-condemnation sentences (often from advice/relationship-conflict contexts) that pass judgment on someone's interpersonal conduct, frequently naming the offending party (e.g. 'her', 'his mom', 'the lady', 'Susan') and pairing them with words like unacceptable, aggressive, entitled, dismissive, or abusive. It does not activate on sentences that merely describe a situation neutrally, offer advice/suggestions, express empathy or validation without a condemnatory verdict, or discuss unrelated factual/logistical content—i.e., sentences lacking a clear negative evaluative judgment of someone's behavior or tone.

title: Enumerated list markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral or bullet token that begins an item in an ordered list, especially early list markers like '2.' or '3.' (often bolded), typically in advice-style responses that break down pros/cons, reasons, or considerations into numbered points. It activates on the digit-plus-period token itself (and sometimes an accompanying bold marker) regardless of the topical content that follows, as seen in the many top-activating examples that are just '2.' or '3.'. It does not activate on ordinary prose sentences without such list formatting, nor on introductory phrases like 'Here's why:' unless followed by the actual numbered marker, and it distinguishes itself from a general 'list-writing' latent by specifically tracking the enumerator token rather than the list's semantic content.

title: Formulaic self-affirmation closer
description: This latent fires on stock, formulaic reassurance phrases that close out advice-giving text, especially the 'Remember, you deserve/are strong/take care of yourself' template used in relationship or emotional-support advice. It activates most strongly on short, templated affirmations that directly address the reader as 'you' with generic uplifting claims about their worth, strength, or deservingness of love/respect/happiness, often beginning with 'Remember,' 'You deserve,' 'You are,' or 'Take care of yourself.' It is largely indifferent to specific topical content and instead responds to the ritualized, boilerplate phrasing and cadence of these closing affirmations, even firing on sentence fragments like 'Be' or 'Keep' that are truncations of this template. It does NOT activate strongly on substantive advice, situational analysis, or reasoning about a specific relationship problem (e.g., discussions of boundaries, trust, or specific actions to take), even when those sentences share similar vocabulary (respect, boundaries, self-care) but lack the direct second-person affirmational/reassurance framing.

title: AITA verdict-seeking closer
description: This latent fires most strongly on the stock closing question "So, AITA?" that ends Reddit-style moral-judgment posts, where the writer explicitly solicits a verdict on whether they were the asshole. More weakly, it activates on related material within the same genre: statements rendering or discussing a verdict (NTA/YTA judgments), phrases like "here's why" preceding a judgment's justification, and hedged moral assessments ("I think you're not the asshole," "a solid 6 or 7 on the Would-I-Be-The-Asshole scale"). It is not simply about advice or empathy in general -- generic supportive statements, practical suggestions, or unrelated question-asking (e.g., "So, what can you do?") activate it far less, since the core trigger is the specific ritualized request-for-judgment framing tied to the AITA format rather than moral reasoning content itself.

title: Offering an alternative option
description: This latent fires on sentences that frame a proposal as a non-mandatory alternative or option for others to consider, often reassuring the listener that it is offered rather than imposed. It activates on language like 'offering an alternative for those who might want to...' where the speaker clarifies the voluntary, optional nature of a suggestion. It would not activate on straightforward commands, mandatory instructions, or neutral factual statements that don't frame something as an optional choice for the listener.

title: Conditional clause opener 'If it'
description: This latent activates on the token sequence "If it", typically at the start of a conditional clause introducing a hypothesis or condition before the consequence is stated. It fires on instances where a sentence or clause begins with this conditional pronoun construction, regardless of the topic being discussed. It would not activate on conditionals phrased differently (e.g., 'If they', 'If the', 'Should it', 'In case it') or on sentences where 'if' appears mid-clause rather than as a clause-initial conditional marker paired with 'it'. The latent is capturing a specific syntactic pattern rather than any semantic content about conditions or hypotheticals in general.

title: Asserting personal boundaries/rights in relationships
description: This latent fires on statements that articulate a person's belief in their right to personal boundaries, autonomy, or respect within an interpersonal relationship, often framed as 'you believe/deserve X, even if it causes discomfort to another.' It activates on second-person or first-person assertions that validate someone's stance on maintaining space, priorities, or values despite potential friction with others (e.g., roommates, family, partners). It would not activate on neutral descriptions of relationships, factual statements about living arrangements, or advice-giving that lacks the framing of an internal belief or entitlement being asserted. It is distinct from general conflict-resolution language, since the core function here is validating or stating a person's justified stance rather than describing the conflict itself or offering steps to resolve it.

title: Empathetic validation opener
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic empathetic phrases that open or frame a supportive response, typically of the form 'That/It/This can be a really [adjective] and [adjective] experience/feeling/situation' or 'I'm so sorry to hear that you're feeling this way,' validating the user's emotional state before any advice is given. It activates most strongly on templated emotional-validation sentences pairing two negative-affect adjectives (tough, painful, frustrating, isolating, overwhelming, confusing) with a noun like feeling, experience, or situation, as well as stock apology/sympathy openers and 'That's a valid/common concern' style acknowledgments. It does NOT activate on the substantive content that follows—concrete advice, situational descriptions, reasoning about the user's specific circumstances, or narrative details about relationships/events—even when those sentences express sympathy or address emotions, since the latent tracks the generic validating-phrase template rather than emotional topic per se.

title: Social approachability advice items
description: This latent fires on formulaic listicle-style advice items recommending friendly social behaviors—smiling, making eye contact, using open/relaxed body language, introducing yourself, being approachable—typically in bolded imperative headers followed by elaboration (e.g., 'Use positive body language**: Make eye contact, smile...'). It also activates on the numbered/bulleted list scaffolding itself (e.g., '2. **', bare 'Be', 'Use') that structurally precedes or introduces such advice, suggesting it tracks this specific template of prescriptive social-skills tips. It does not activate on general relationship or social advice that lacks this smile/eye-contact/body-language approachability framing, nor on reflective, empathetic, or analytical commentary about someone's feelings, motivations, or interpersonal dynamics (as seen in most random examples), even when those also occur in list format.
